stages.title: Advanced grammar
stages.hook: "The window was broken" - who broke it? Why might a speaker leave that out?
explain: The passive voice puts the receiver of an action first: "The window was broken by the ball." It is made with be plus the past participle. We use it when the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious, and in formal or scientific writing.

Conditionals describe real and unreal situations. The second conditional imagines the present: "If I had more time, I would learn Greek." The third conditional imagines the past: "If she had left earlier, she would have caught the train." Modals such as must, might and should express certainty, possibility and advice.
stages.mnemonic: Passive: be + past participle. Third conditional: had + participle, would have + participle.
items: a passive sentence with no named doer
sentences: The letter was written by hand.
If I were you, I would apologise.
She might have missed the bus.

gq.q: Which sentence is in the passive voice?
o: The cake was eaten by the guests.
The guests are eating the cake.
The guests will eat the cake.
gq.why: The passive has be plus the past participle and puts the receiver of the action first.

gq.q: Complete: "If I ___ more time, I would travel more."
gq.why: The second conditional uses a past simple form in the if-clause and would in the main clause.

panel.q: Which sentence is a third conditional?
o: If he had studied, he would have passed.
If he studies, he will pass.
If he studied, he would pass.
panel.why: The third conditional uses had plus participle, then would have plus participle, for unreal past events.

panel.q: Why is "If I was you" often corrected to "If I were you" in formal writing?
o: Were is the subjunctive form for unreal situations
Was is never used in English
panel.why: Formal standard uses were for hypothetical statements, although was is common in speech.

panel.q: When is the passive a good choice?
panel.model: When the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious, or when you want the focus on the object, as in formal or scientific writing.
panel.why: Passive is chosen for focus and style.

teach.model: In the passive, the thing receiving the action comes first: The window was broken. Use be plus the past participle. Conditionals use if. Use had and would have for imagined past events.

points.ask: How do I make the passive?
How do I talk about the imagined past?

stages.title: Complex sentence patterns
stages.hook: How can one sentence hold three ideas without sounding messy?
explain: Advanced writers combine clauses to show relationships: cause (since, as), purpose (so that, in order to), concession (even though, whereas) and time (as soon as, by the time). Relative clauses can be defining ("The man who called is my uncle") or non-defining, with commas ("My uncle, who lives in Perth, called").

Reported speech moves a tense back: "I am tired" becomes "She said she was tired." Inversion is used for emphasis: "Never have I seen such a view." Parallel structure keeps lists balanced: "She likes swimming, cycling and hiking."
stages.mnemonic: A comma-clause is a bonus; a defining clause is essential.
sentences: She said that she was tired.
My uncle, who lives in Perth, called.
Never have I seen such a view.

gq.q: Which sentence has a non-defining relative clause?
o: My sister, who lives in Lagos, is a doctor.
The woman who lives next door is a doctor.
The book that I read was long.
gq.why: Extra information is set off with commas and can be removed without changing the core meaning.

gq.q: Change to reported speech: "I am hungry," he said.
o: He said that he was hungry.
He said that he is hungry now yesterday.
gq.why: In backshifted reported speech the present becomes past and the pronoun changes.

panel.q: Which list is parallel?
o: She enjoys reading, writing and painting.
She enjoys reading, to write and painting.
She enjoys to read, writing and paint.
She enjoys read, writes and paintings.
panel.why: Each item uses the same grammatical form (-ing).

panel.q: "Hardly had we arrived when it began to rain." What is special here?
o: Inversion after a negative adverb for emphasis
panel.why: After hardly and similar negative adverbs the auxiliary comes before the subject.

panel.q: What is the difference between "although" and "whereas"?
panel.model: Although introduces an unexpected contrast within one idea; whereas contrasts two different things or people.
panel.why: Concession and contrast.

teach.model: Join ideas with linking words that show cause, contrast or time. A defining clause is needed. A non-defining clause adds extra information between commas.

stages.title: Extended conversations
stages.hook: How do you politely disagree with someone and keep talking?
explain: Extended conversations need discourse markers. "Well", "actually", "by the way" and "anyway" manage turns and topics. Use hedging to soften opinions: "I think it might be..." "It seems to me..."

To disagree politely: "I see what you mean, but..." or "That's true, although..." To clarify: "Do you mean...?" To keep a topic going, ask open questions: "What do you think about...?" and use backchannel sounds like "mm" and "right".
stages.mnemonic: Soften, link, ask: hedge your view, link to theirs, ask a question.
items: I see what you mean, but
sentences: I see what you mean, but I disagree.
What do you make of the new plan?

gq.q: Which sounds the most tactful way to disagree?
o: I see your point, but I'm not sure it's quite right.
gq.why: Acknowledging the other view first, then softening, keeps rapport.
It signals a related or unrelated aside.

panel.q: Why do speakers say "kind of" or "sort of"?
o: To hedge and make a claim less absolute
Because they are unsure of grammar
panel.why: These are softening devices.

panel.q: Why do speakers use backchannel sounds such as "mm" and "right"?
panel.model: They show the speaker you are listening and encourage them to continue.
panel.why: Backchannelling supports interaction.

panel.q: Which reply shows active listening?
o: So you moved to Toronto last year? What was that like?
panel.why: Paraphrasing and following up show interest.

teach.model: Show you are listening with words like right and mm. Soften opinions with I think or it seems. Disagree politely by first saying what you agree with. Ask open questions.

points.ask: How do I show I am listening?
How do I give an opinion politely?

stages.title: Formal and informal registers
stages.hook: You write to your best friend and to a company boss. Should the language be the same?
explain: Register is the level of formality. Formal English avoids contractions and slang, and uses full verbs: "I would like to enquire" instead of "I wanna ask". Informal English uses contractions, phrasal verbs and slang: "Can you check this out?"
Phrasal verbs are often informal, with a formal equivalent: get in touch = contact, find out = discover, look into = investigate, put off = postpone. Choose register by audience, purpose and medium.
stages.mnemonic: Know your audience: boss in a suit, friend in a T-shirt.
sentences: We regret to inform you of the delay.
Sorry, the meeting's been called off.
I am writing to enquire about the job.

o: I am writing to request information.
gq.why: Formal register uses full forms and polite, precise phrases.

gq.q: What is a formal word for "look into"?
gq.why: Look into a problem means investigate it.

panel.q: What does "put off" mean in "The meeting was put off"?
panel.why: Put off means postpone to a later time.

panel.q: Why should a job application avoid slang and contractions?
panel.model: Formal register makes a professional impression and shows respect for the reader.
panel.why: Appropriateness depends on context.

panel.q: Which is a phrasal verb?
panel.why: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a particle, like take off.

teach.model: Register means how formal your language is. Use full forms and polite words for bosses and strangers. Use contractions and phrasal verbs with friends. Think of who will read it.

stages.title: Reading articles and literature
stages.hook: A headline says "Mayor Quits Over Budget Row". Why do headlines sound so short?
explain: Newspaper articles follow a pattern: headline, lead (the key facts), details and quotes. Headlines drop small words and use the present tense for past events. Literature uses more figurative language: metaphor, simile and symbol.

Good readers ask about the author's purpose, tone and audience. Tone is the attitude of the writer, which can be seen in word choice. Distinguish between fact and opinion, and between what the text says and what you infer.
stages.mnemonic: Lead with who, what, when, where, why: the five Ws.
items: the title of a news story
the first paragraph, with key facts
a comparison using like or as
a comparison without like or as
something that stands for an idea
sentences: She was as brave as a lion.
The report was published on Monday.

gq.q: "Her voice was music" is an example of...
gq.why: It states directly that her voice is music, with no like or as.
It uses as ... as to compare.

panel.q: Which is an opinion rather than a fact?
o: This is the best film of the year.
The film was shot in Spain.
panel.why: Best is a judgement that cannot be proved by evidence alone.

panel.q: How can you tell the tone of a text?
panel.model: Look at the writer's word choice and style to see the attitude, such as humorous, angry or formal.
panel.why: Tone comes from diction.

panel.q: Why do headlines say "Team Wins Cup" instead of "A team has won the cup"?
o: They save space and sound dramatic
panel.why: Headline style drops articles and uses the present tense.

teach.model: A news article tells the main facts first. Literature uses images like similes and metaphors. Ask what the author wants and what the tone is. Keep fact and opinion apart.

points.ask: How do I tell fact from opinion?
What should I ask about the author?

stages.title: Essay and correspondence writing
stages.hook: What makes the difference between an essay that persuades and one that wanders?
explain: An essay has an introduction with a thesis (the main claim), body paragraphs each with a point, evidence and explanation, and a conclusion. Linking words (moreover, in contrast, consequently) connect the argument.

A formal letter begins "Dear Mr Okafor," or "Dear Sir or Madam," and ends "Yours sincerely," if you know the name, and "Yours faithfully," if you do not (British style). American letters often end "Sincerely,". State the purpose in the first paragraph. Revise for clarity.
items: the main claim of an essay
to begin a letter to an unknown person
to end when you know the name (UK)
to end when you do not know the name (UK)
sentences: I am writing to apply for the post.

gq.q: Which ending goes with "Dear Sir or Madam" in British English?
gq.why: The convention pairs an unknown recipient with faithfully.

gq.q: What is the thesis of an essay?
gq.why: Everything in the essay supports the thesis.

panel.q: Which sentence is the strongest thesis?
o: Schools should start later because teenagers need more sleep.
panel.why: A thesis takes a clear, arguable position and gives a reason.

panel.q: Why is evidence needed in a body paragraph?
panel.model: Evidence supports the claim and persuades the reader that it is reasonable.
panel.why: An argument without evidence is only an opinion.

panel.q: Which opening is best for a complaint email?
o: I am writing to complain about the damaged item I received on 3 May.
To whom it may concern, hello.
panel.why: It states the purpose clearly and politely with a specific detail.

teach.model: An essay needs a thesis, body paragraphs with evidence, and a conclusion. In a letter, state your purpose early. Use Dear Sir or Madam with Yours faithfully in British English.

points.ask: How do I begin a letter?

stages.title: Translation fundamentals
stages.hook: Why can't you translate "It's raining cats and dogs" word by word into another language?
explain: Translation is about meaning, not single words. False friends are words that look similar in two languages but differ in meaning. For example, Spanish "embarazada" means pregnant, not embarrassed, and English "actual" does not mean current.

Translators choose between literal and free translation. Idioms must usually be replaced by an equivalent idiom or explained. Context, register and audience guide each choice. Always check collocations: in English we make a mistake, but do homework.
stages.mnemonic: Translate the message, not the words.
items: a word that looks like one in another language but differs in meaning
a sentence read aloud in another language
sentences: He does his homework every day.
The idiom cannot be translated literally.

gq.q: Which is the natural English collocation?

o: A look-alike word with a different meaning
gq.why: False friends mislead learners because they resemble words in their own language.

panel.q: Why is "I have 20 years" a typical learner error from some languages?
o: The learner translates the structure of their own language
English has no word for years
panel.why: English uses be for age: I am 20 years old.

panel.q: When should a translator prefer meaning over literal wording?
panel.model: For idioms and cultural expressions, because a literal version would be unnatural or confusing to the reader.
panel.why: Natural equivalence.

panel.q: "Eventually" in English means...
panel.why: Eventually means finally; it is a false friend of eventual- words in several languages.

teach.model: Good translation keeps the meaning, not just the words. Beware of false friends. Replace idioms with natural phrases. Think about context and the reader.

stages.title: Regional varieties and cultural context
stages.hook: A Briton says "pavement" and an Australian says "footpath". Is anyone wrong?
explain: English has many standard varieties. British English (BrE) and American English (AmE) differ in vocabulary (lift/elevator, flat/apartment, boot/trunk), spelling (colour/color, centre/center, travelled/traveled) and some grammar (BrE "have you got", AmE "do you have").

Other varieties include Australian, Canadian, Indian, Nigerian and Jamaican English. No variety is more correct; all are valid within their communities. Choose one consistently in your writing and know the differences.
stages.mnemonic: Lift or elevator, both go up: different words, same ride.
items: British word for an apartment building floor home
American word for a sweet cookie
sentences: I live in a flat in London.
We took the elevator to the tenth floor.

gq.why: American English uses -er in words like center.
The boot is the car luggage space, which Americans call the trunk.

panel.q: A learner writes "colour" in one line and "organize" with z in another. What is best?
o: Choose one variety and stay consistent
panel.why: Consistency in spelling is expected; note that -ize is also accepted in Oxford British spelling.

panel.q: Why is no variety of English "more correct" than another?
panel.model: Each variety is a valid standard for its community; they differ in usage, not in correctness.
panel.why: Linguists describe variation neutrally.

panel.q: A business in Mumbai sends an email in Indian English. What is the best attitude?
o: Accept it as a legitimate variety and focus on clarity
panel.why: World Englishes are legitimate; clarity is the shared goal.

teach.topic: British and American English and beyond
teach.model: English has regional varieties. British and American English differ in some words, spellings and grammar. There are other varieties such as Australian and Indian English. All of them are correct for their speakers.

stages.title: Structured debates and presentations
stages.hook: What makes a talk of five minutes stick in the audience's mind?
explain: A presentation has an opening that hooks, a clear structure, signposts ("First... Second... To sum up...") and a strong close. Use short sentences, pauses and eye contact. Keep each slide to one idea.

A debate asks you to take a side. State a claim, give a reason and evidence, then answer counter-arguments: "Some may argue that... However..." Stay respectful. Attack the argument, not the person (avoid ad hominem).
stages.mnemonic: Tell them what you will say, say it, tell them what you said.
items: to start with a question or story
a word that guides the listener
to speak against a person, not a point
sentences: First, I will explain the problem.
Some may argue that this is too costly.
To sum up, we should act now.

gq.q: What does a signpost phrase like "Firstly" do?
o: Guides the listener through the structure

gq.q: Which is a respectful way to challenge a point in a debate?
o: I understand your point, but the evidence suggests otherwise.
gq.why: It deals with the argument politely.

panel.q: Which is an ad hominem argument?
o: You cannot trust his proposal because he is young.
His data are out of date.
panel.why: It attacks the person rather than the idea.

panel.q: Why should a speaker answer counter-arguments?
panel.model: It shows that you have thought about the other side and makes your own argument more convincing.
panel.why: Rebuttal strengthens credibility.

panel.q: How many ideas should a slide ideally have?
panel.why: A slide with a single idea is easier for the audience to follow.

teach.topic: Giving a talk and joining a debate
teach.model: Open with a hook, use signposts like first and finally, and close strongly. In a debate, make a claim, support it with reasons and evidence, and answer the other side politely.

points.ask: How do I guide the audience?
How do I handle a debate?
